planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in moist, loamy, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade.

directions: Fire Storm is a dwarfed improvement on the older 'Fireball' selection, packing the same semi-double orange flowers onto a much more compact, non-sprawling clump. It blooms over an unusually long stretch from spring into early fall rather than tapering off after a single early flush. Keep the soil evenly moist and avoid letting the crown dry out for best repeat bloom, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring. Deadheading spent stems helps sustain flowering and keeps the mound tidy for cutting or border use.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in moist, loamy, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade.

directions: Sunkissed Lime pairs bright lime-and-yellow foliage with orange flowers held on unusually short stems, giving it two seasons of color rather than relying on bloom alone. It is most floriferous in spring, tapering off by early summer, after which the chartreuse foliage mound carries the display. Keep soil consistently moist in average garden conditions and divide every few years to maintain vigor. Its low, fast-spreading clump suits edging and border fronts where the foliage color can read from a distance.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in moist, loamy, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade.

directions: Tempo Fiesta opens bright yellow flowers rimmed in vivid orange picotee edging over a mounding clump of clean, deep green foliage. Part of the TEMPO series bred for neater, more weed-smothering growth than older geums, it flowers heavily in spring and often rebounds with a second flush in fall. Keep soil evenly moist through the growing season and shear back after the first bloom flush to encourage the fall repeat. Hummingbirds and other pollinators visit regularly while it is in flower.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade once frost danger has passed.

directions: Colorburst Rose produces an abundance of tubular, intensely purple-rose flowers on an upright, mounding plant from late spring through fall. Unlike older Cape fuchsias that spread by suckering, this selection stays put, making it easier to use as a defined color accent in a border or large container. It tolerates heat and, once established, drought reasonably well, needing only occasional deep watering between rains. Hummingbirds visit the tubular blooms steadily through the long flowering season.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade once frost danger has passed.

directions: Colorburst Yellow carries soft yellow, tubular flowers above pine-green foliage on a compact, non-spreading mound, blooming steadily from late spring through fall. It needs sharp winter drainage to survive in its hardiness range, since wet, cold soil is more damaging than cold air alone. Allow the soil to dry somewhat between waterings once the plant is established rather than keeping it continually wet. The long bloom season draws a steady stream of hummingbirds and other pollinators.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; a period of cold exposure over winter improves the following spring's bloom.

directions: Luna opens double, pompom-form flowers that start pure yellow, pass through a yellow-and-white stage, and finish nearly white, so a single clump shows several color phases over its bloom run. It flowers from early to midsummer on an upright, dense mound and can bloom in its first year from a spring planting. Divide every few years in spring to keep the clump vigorous, and deadhead spent stems to tidy the display. It tolerates average garden soil well as long as drainage is reasonable.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Sugar Bowl is an unusually low Shasta daisy, forming a wide, flat mound only a few inches tall that disappears under layered, multi-petaled white flowers from late spring into summer. Its tight branching means new buds keep opening in succession over a long bloom window rather than flowering all at once. It handles summer heat notably well for the genus, making it a good front-of-border or container choice in warmer climates. Deadhead regularly and divide every few years to keep the dense mound from thinning at the center.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun.

directions: Dynomite forms an extremely short, dense mound of dusky purple-red foliage topped with large heads of deep rose-red flowers in late summer. Its tight, sturdy habit holds up without flopping, an improvement over older dark-leaved stonecrops it was bred to surpass. Grow in lean, fast-draining soil, since excess moisture and rich soil both encourage floppy, less floriferous growth. It needs minimal water once established and is a strong late-season draw for bees and butterflies.
